newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden investigates incursions by spy subs.
newsitem.headline: Sweden investigates incursions by spy subs.

text.p: Sweden, which has already confessed to mistakenly confusing swimming mink for Soviet submarines, said on Wednesday it was investigating other spy sub incursions into its waters - possibly by western vessels.
A confidential report was presented to Sweden's foreign policy advisory committee on Wednesday about incursions into Swedish waters, but the details were kept secret.
Foreign Minister Lena Hjelm-Wallen made no comment on a report in Swedish newspaper Svenska Dagbladet that said the submarines in question were from western countries.
"It's not possible to draw any conclusion about which country or countries are behind the U-boat infringements of Swedish waters," she told reporters after the committee meeting.
"We have a continual job in the committee to look at possible reasons for U-boat incursions."
This is the first time that there has been a suggestion of western powers sending spy subs into Swedish waters.
However neutral Sweden and its neighbour, NATO member Norway, frequently reported supposed sightings and contact with Russian submarines in the 1980s and early 1990s before the end of the Cold War.
Between 1980 and 1992 Sweden poured three billion crowns -- worth about $480 million at the time -- into the hunt for foreign submarines in the Swedish Baltic archipelago.
The expenditure was considered necessary after a Soviet Whiskey class submarine ran aground near a Swedish naval base in the southern town of Karlskrona in 1981.
Moscow blamed a navigational error on what became known as the Whisky on the Rocks affair.
But Sweden was left red-faced last year when it was revealed that its submarine-hunters since 1992 had been battling swimming minks - not Russian submarines.
The minks, amphibious mammals which are common in Sweden, have a sonar trail that resemble a submarine.
Hjelm-Wallen said the foreign policy advisory committee, that includes Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustav and meets at the Royal Palace in Stockholm, kept a constant watch for submarines.
